title: Simulation Task
description: Develop a multi-agent simulation system that models the spread of mask-wearing behavior through social networks.
simulation_focus: Predict agents' mask-wearing behavior over day 30 - day 39 (last ten days) based on their attributes, social connections, and past behavior
Model information propagation and behavioral changes triggered by social influence and government intervention starting on Day 10

data_files.agent_attributes.csv: Contains demographic and behavioral attributes of each agent, including age, occupation, risk perception, and social connection counts
data_files.social_network.json: Contains structured data representing a social network. Each entry corresponds to a user (identified by a unique integer ID), and the values describe the different types of relationships that user has with others. Data Structure: The top-level structure is a dictionary ({} in JSON). Keys: Each key is a unique user ID (as an integer, e.g., 0, 1, 2, etc.). Values: Each value is another dictionary with the following fields: "family": a list of user IDs representing family connections. "work_school": a list of user IDs representing colleagues or schoolmates. "community": a list of user IDs representing community-level acquaintances. "all": a merged list of all user IDs connected to the user across the three categories above.
data_files.train_data.csv: Time series data for the first 30 days, used for training the model

RMSE.description: Root Mean Square Error measuring overall predictive accuracy of mask adoption rates
RMSE.interpretation: Directly interpretable as percentage deviations due to the 0-1 range

Peak Adoption Rate Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting maximum mask adoption during intervention

Time-to-Peak Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting the time lag from intervention to peak behavior change

key_patterns.name: Degree consistency across layers
key_patterns.description: For most agents, total_connections equals the sum of family_connections + work_school_connections + community_connections. Occasional mismatches likely indicate data entry error or rounding when anonymized.
key_patterns.relevance: Ensures valid degree sequences for network generation; mismatches must be corrected or handled to avoid stubs imbalance in configuration models.

key_patterns.name: Layer-specific degree heterogeneity
key_patterns.description: Family degrees are low with a narrow spread; work/school degrees vary by occupation/age (students and white-collar tend to have more ties than retirees); community degrees are broader and more right-skewed.
key_patterns.relevance: Supports using different degree distributions per layer and higher influence weighting for family due to denser clustering and repeated contact.

key_patterns.name: Risk perception is bounded and likely bimodal-to-skewed
key_patterns.description: risk_perception in [0,1] often clusters around moderate and high values with a long tail to low risk, well-modeled by a Beta distribution.
key_patterns.relevance: Directly informs heterogeneity in susceptibility/thresholds for mask adoption.

key_patterns.name: Initial mask-wearing varies by demographics
key_patterns.description: initial_mask_wearing rates increase with age_group and among health-conscious occupations; students may start lower unless mandates exist.
key_patterns.relevance: Sets realistic initial conditions and subgroup-specific baseline adoption parameters.

key_patterns.name: Layer overlap in multiplex network
key_patterns.description: Neighbors can appear across multiple layers (e.g., family who are also coworkers). The “all” neighbor list is de-duplicated; overlap can be quantified via Jaccard indices between layer neighbor sets.
key_patterns.relevance: Prevents double-counting influence and supports weighted aggregation across layers.

key_patterns.name: Undirected but asymmetric listings
key_patterns.description: social_network.json is intended undirected, but some edges may be listed for one agent and not reciprocated for the other.
key_patterns.relevance: Symmetrization is required for consistent influence computation.

key_patterns.name: Homophily by age and occupation
key_patterns.description: Family edges are strongly within-household age bands; work/school shows strong occupation-based clustering; community is more mixed.
key_patterns.relevance: Enables assortative mixing matrices in synthetic network generation and subgroup-targeted interventions.

key_patterns.name: Temporal persistence and relapse in mask-wearing
key_patterns.description: Panel data show high persistence P(1→1) and lower but non-zero relapse P(1→0); adoption P(0→1) increases with received_info exposure.
key_patterns.relevance: Calibrates Markov transition dynamics and the exogenous information effect.

key_patterns.name: Peer influence effect
key_patterns.description: An agent’s probability of wearing a mask at t increases with the lagged fraction of neighbors wearing masks, strongest in family, then work/school, then community.
key_patterns.relevance: Calibrates layer-specific social influence weights or logistic coefficients.

key_distributions.name: Family degree distribution
key_distributions.parameters: Negative Binomial with mean mu_fam and dispersion k_fam; estimate mu_fam = mean(family_connections), Var informs k_fam via Var = mu + mu^2/k.

key_distributions.name: Work/School degree distribution
key_distributions.description: Occupation- and age-dependent degrees with higher means for students and white-collar.
key_distributions.parameters: Negative Binomial by subgroup: NB(mu_ws[group], k_ws[group]). Fit separate parameters for occupation-age strata.

key_distributions.name: Community degree distribution
key_distributions.description: Right-skewed with heavier tail than other layers.
key_distributions.parameters: Negative Binomial NB(mu_com, k_com) or Zero-Inflated NB if many zeros.

key_distributions.name: Total connections
key_distributions.description: Approximately the sum across layers; used as a consistency check.
key_distributions.parameters: mu_total ≈ mu_fam + mu_ws + mu_com; validate row-wise equality.

key_distributions.name: Risk perception
key_distributions.parameters: Beta(alpha, beta); compute alpha = m*(m*(1-m)/v - 1), beta = (1-m)*(m*(1-m)/v - 1) from sample mean m and variance v of risk_perception.

key_distributions.name: Initial mask-wearing by subgroup
key_distributions.description: Bernoulli rates stratified by age_group and occupation.

key_distributions.name: Information exposure per day
key_distributions.description: Probability an agent receives info on a day.
key_distributions.parameters: pi_info[day or group] = mean(received_info_t); model as Bernoulli with day fixed effects or Poisson process if counts are available.

key_distributions.name: Adoption and persistence transitions
key_distributions.description: First-order Markov transitions with possible conditioning on info exposure.
key_distributions.parameters: p11 = P(1→1), p10 = 1 - p11, p01 = P(0→1), p00 = 1 - p01; also p01_info = P(0→1 | received_info=1), p01_noinfo = P(0→1 | received_info=0).

key_distributions.name: Layer overlap
key_distributions.description: Overlap between layer neighbor sets per agent.
key_distributions.parameters: Jaccard indices J(fam,work), J(fam,com), J(work,com); distribution summarized by mean and IQR.

key_relationships.relationship: Positive association; higher risk perception correlates with higher probability of initial mask use.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate via logistic regression; report odds ratio per 0.1 increase in risk_perception.

key_relationships.relationship: Students/Young have higher work/school connections; retirees have near-zero.
key_relationships.strength: Strong; test via ANOVA or regression with large effect sizes expected.

key_relationships.relationship: White-collar and student occupations show higher degrees than blue-collar and unemployed/retired.
key_relationships.strength: Moderate to strong; subgroup means differ significantly.

key_relationships.relationship: Positive peer effect; stronger in family than work/school, weakest in community.
key_relationships.strength: Quantify via logistic coefficients beta_fam > beta_work > beta_comm; check with standardized effects.

key_relationships.relationship: Information exposure increases adoption probability and persistence.
key_relationships.strength: Moderate; compute Average Treatment Effect on the Treated: ATT = p(1|info) - p(1|no_info) conditional on t-1 state.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher-degree agents may receive more information (if info propagates socially) or be more likely targeted.
key_relationships.strength: Weak to moderate; assess via correlation or logistic regression controlling for group.

key_relationships.relationship: High agreement if JSON is derived from CSV; discrepancies indicate generation noise or missing reciprocation.
key_relationships.strength: Expect high; compute per-layer correlation and RMSE.

network_source.value: Use social_network.json as the primary network; if absent, synthesize per layer via configuration model from CSV degree sequences
network_source.notes: When synthesizing, enforce even stub sums per layer; apply assortative rewiring to match age/occupation mixing.

symmetrize_edges.notes: Make edges undirected by adding missing reciprocals and removing self-loops.

layer_weights.source: Behavioral calibration from panel with peer effects; defaults reflect stronger familial influence
layer_weights.notes: Estimate from logistic coefficients or contact frequency; normalize to sum to 1.

assortativity_mixing.value: Estimate 3x3 age_group and occupation mixing matrices per layer
assortativity_mixing.notes: Use these matrices during synthetic network generation to preserve homophily.

clustering_target.notes: If generating networks, add triangle-closing rewiring to match observed clustering coefficients.

baseline_persistence_p11.notes: Compute by subgroup; if using logistic model include previous state term.

baseline_adoption_p01.notes: This is the base hazard absent info or peer effects.

info_effect.value: Delta in adoption and persistence when received_info_t=1 (e.g., p01_info - p01_noinfo)
info_effect.notes: Estimate separately for 0→1 and 1→1 transitions; may vary by layer if info is layer-specific.

peer_effect_coefficients.source: Panel CSV joined with network; logistic regression on lagged neighbor_mask_rate by layer
peer_effect_coefficients.notes: Use lagged neighbor states to reduce simultaneity; standardize by layer to compare effect sizes.

risk_perception_weight.notes: Include interaction terms with peer effects if higher risk moderates social susceptibility.

relapse_probability.notes: Estimate by subgroup; often small but non-zero.

threshold_distribution.value: Map risk_perception to adoption threshold theta_i ~ Beta(alpha, beta) or linear theta_i = 1 - risk_perception_i
threshold_distribution.notes: Alternative to logistic contagion; calibrate alpha,beta to match adoption curves.

p_info_daily.notes: Allow day and subgroup heterogeneity; model as Bernoulli with day fixed effects.

info_target_layers.source: Policy design; data suggests mandates often at work/school
info_target_layers.notes: If simulating mandates, apply as exogenous constraint on these layers.

info_decay.value: geometric decay with half-life H days
info_decay.notes: If received_info has lingering effects, include a decayed cumulative exposure variable.

initial_state_source.value: Prefer panel day=0 wearing_mask; fallback to agent CSV initial_mask_wearing
initial_state_source.notes: Resolve conflicts by prioritizing the time-indexed panel.

risk_perception_params.value: Beta(alpha, beta) fitted to observed risk_perception
risk_perception_params.notes: For agents with missing risk, impute from subgroup Beta posterior.

subgroup_effects.value: Age_group and occupation fixed effects in behavior model
subgroup_effects.notes: Capture systematic differences in baseline adoption and peer sensitivity.

agent_random_effects.notes: Accounts for unobserved individual propensity; improves calibration robustness.

preprocessing_steps.purpose: Ensure family + work_school + community equals total_connections; coerce negatives to zero; flag and fix mismatches.
Convert social_network.json keys to int; ensure neighbor lists are ints; align with agent_id domain.
Make the network undirected and remove self-loops; ensure no double counting across layers when aggregating influence.
Attach demographics and risk_perception to each node for stratified analysis and modeling.
For each agent-day, compute fraction of neighbors wearing masks at t-1 by layer to use as regressors.
Verify day indices are consecutive per agent; impute or drop missing days with clear rules.
Identify agents with zero degree across layers; handle as purely exogenous adoption (no peer effect).
Derive occupation-age groups for stratified degree fitting and behavior modeling.

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Two-stage calibration. Stage 1 (Network): If using social_network.json, compute empirical per-layer degree distributions, clustering, and mixing matrices; if synthesizing, fit Negative Binomial parameters by subgroup per layer and generate networks via configuration model with assortative rewiring to match mixing and approximate clustering. Stage 2 (Behavior): Fit a logistic GLMM for wearing_mask_t with predictors: previous state, received_info_t, lagged neighbor_mask_rate by layer, risk_perception, age_group, occupation, and interactions (e.g., student × work layer). Include agent random intercepts to capture unobserved heterogeneity. Use lagged peer variables to mitigate simultaneity bias; optionally include day fixed effects. Translate fitted coefficients into simulation parameters: baseline transition probabilities, layer weights or coefficients, and risk-threshold mapping. As an alternative, calibrate a threshold model by fitting a Beta distribution over thresholds such that simulated adoption curves match observed time-series.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Multi-level validation. 1) Micro-level: Hold out a time window; assess predictive accuracy (AUC, Brier score) of daily wearing_mask states; compare estimated vs. simulated transition probabilities by subgroup. 2) Meso-level: Compare simulated vs. observed adoption time-series (mean and variance) and subgroup adoption trajectories; check persistence and relapse rates. 3) Network-level: Validate influence patterns by correlating simulated peer effects with empirical coefficients; reproduce cascade sizes and temporal clustering. 4) Structural: If synthesizing networks, compare degree distributions, clustering coefficients, and mixing matrices with targets. 5) Sensitivity: Vary key parameters (peer coefficients, info effect, layer weights) and verify qualitative robustness. Use cross-validation across days and bootstrap CIs for parameters.
key_variables_to_calibrate: Layer-specific peer effect coefficients (beta_fam, beta_work, beta_comm)
Risk perception effect (beta_risk) and threshold distribution parameters (Beta alpha,beta)
Information exposure probability (pi_info) and its effect size (delta_info)
Layer weights for influence aggregation (w_family, w_work, w_community)
Assortativity/mixing matrices by age_group and occupation per layer
Relapse probability P(1→0) and its determinants
Clustering targets per layer for synthetic network generation

file_summaries:
- Overall structure/type:
  - CSV file; each row = one agent (flat records, no nesting).
  - Columns mix of identifiers, demographics, behavioral state, and degree counts for network layers.

- Columns (semantics):
  - agent_id: unique integer key for each agent.
  - age: integer; raw age.
  - age_group: categorical bucket of age (e.g., Youth, Young Adult, Middle Age).
  - occupation: categorical (e.g., Student, Blue Collar, White Collar); informs work/school layer membership.
  - risk_perception: float in [0,1]; intrinsic propensity to wear masks given perceived risk.
  - initial_mask_wearing: boolean; initial behavioral state at t0.
  - family_connections, work_school_connections, community_connections: integers; desired degree per social layer.
  - total_connections: integer; typically equals the sum of layer-specific connections (sanity check).

- Relationships / structure:
  - No explicit edges; connection fields are counts (degree sequence) per layer, implying a multiplex (family, work/school, community) network.
  - total_connections aggregates the three layer counts; verify consistency per row.
  - Implicit constraints:
    - Students and school-aged agents should have work_school layer ties; retirees may have zero there.
    - Family layer spans across age groups; community layer is general.

- Use in simulation design:
  - Initialize agent nodes with attributes: demographics, risk_perception, and initial_mask_wearing.
  - Generate three-layer social network using the per-layer degree sequences (e.g., configuration model per layer), then combine into a multiplex/weighted network.
  - Use layer types to weight influence (e.g., stronger influence within family; medium at work/school; variable in community).
  - Behavior update rules:
    - Social influence depends on mask adoption among neighbors (possibly per-layer weighted).
    - Individual susceptibility/threshold modulated by risk_perception, age_group, and occupation (e.g., students influenced more by school peers).
  - Validation/checks:
    - Ensure nonnegative integer degrees; total_connections ≈ sum of layer degrees.
    - Handle agents with zero degree (isolates).
    - Keep risk_perception within [0,1] and initial_mask_wearing as boolean.

Concise semantic metadata summary for social_network.json

- Overall data structure and type
  - JSON object representing a static, multiplex (multi-layer) social network.
  - Top-level: mapping from agent IDs (as strings) to their neighborhood lists by layer.
  - Layer lists are arrays of integer agent IDs (neighbors).

- Meaning of keys or columns
  - "<agent_id>": a unique agent/node identifier (stringified; neighbors are ints).
  - family: close-tie household/family connections for the agent.
  - work_school: coworkers/classmates connections.
  - community: broader community/social contacts.
  - all: the union of family ∪ work_school ∪ community for the agent (appears de-duplicated).

- Relationships or nested elements
  - Each agent maps to an object containing four arrays; these arrays are neighbor lists for that agent on distinct layers.
  - The network is likely undirected in practice, but directionality is not enforced; reciprocity should be validated if needed.
  - Layers are disjoint categories but may overlap in members; “all” prevents double counting only within an agent’s list.
  - IDs appear to span 0–999 (1000 agents); keys are strings while neighbor IDs are integers—normalize types when indexing.
  - Edges are unweighted in the file; no timestamps—this is a static snapshot; no self-loops observed.

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agents: one agent per top-level key; augment with behavioral state (e.g., wears_mask: True/False), susceptibility to influence, thresholds, and compliance propensity—these are not provided.
  - Interaction topology: use the three layers as distinct influence channels with layer-specific contact frequencies or influence weights (e.g., family > work_school > community).
  - Update dynamics: at each timestep, an agent’s mask-wearing state can be updated based on neighbors’ states aggregated by layer (e.g., weighted fraction/threshold, contagion probability).
  - Scheduling:
    - Layered interactions: sample contacts per layer with different probabilities to reflect tie strength.
    - Or build an aggregated graph from “all” with weights derived from layer membership to avoid double counting.
  - Seeding and interventions: select initial adopters by layer (e.g., seed families or workplaces) and simulate policies (e.g., workplace mandates affecting the work_school layer only).
  - Data handling cautions:
    - Convert keys to ints or neighbor IDs to strings for consistent lookups.
    - If treating the network as undirected, optionally symmetrize edges.
    - Ensure no duplicate neighbor influence when combining layers; either use “all” once with weights or keep layers separate.

- Overall structure and type:
  - CSV in long/panel format: one row per (day, agent) observation.
  - Likely primary key: (day, agent_id). No nesting; flat schema.

- Columns and meanings:
  - day (int): discrete time step (t = 0,1,2,…) for the simulation.
  - agent_id (int): unique identifier of an agent; repeats across days.
  - wearing_mask (bool): agent’s behavioral state at day t.
  - received_info (bool): whether the agent was exposed to information (e.g., message/campaign) on day t.

- Relationships/nested elements:
  - Temporal dependency within agent_id across consecutive days; suitable for Markov/transition modeling.
  - No explicit social network edges or group labels present; network must be provided elsewhere or synthesized.
  - No nested structures; relationships are inferred via time and repeated agent_id.

- How this informs simulation entities/interactions:
  - Agents: instantiate one agent per unique agent_id with state variables wearing_mask and received_info that update each tick (day).
  - Initialization: use day 0 rows to set initial mask-wearing states (and initial info exposure if present).
  - Dynamics/parameters:
    - Estimate transition probabilities P(wearing_mask_t | wearing_mask_{t-1}, received_info_t, …) from the panel to calibrate behavior adoption, persistence, and relapse.
    - Model the effect of received_info as an exogenous shock increasing adoption probability and/or persistence.
    - If adding social contagion, combine calibrated baseline transitions with peer influence from the network (e.g., function of neighbors’ mask rate), since network structure is not in this file.
  - Validation: compare simulated time series of wearing_mask per agent or aggregate adoption curves against the empirical panel to assess fit.
  - Data handling notes: parse booleans correctly; ensure continuity of day indices per agent; handle agents/days not observed (missing rows) explicitly in the simulation setup.
